# Medicine Origins Atlas: data and related reading

Source-linked histories of 115 drug classes in a selected inventory of 226 medication groups from the United States and England. Medicine names point to class histories with explicit lineage, source-access and uncertainty limits.

## Fetch a medicine's history

1. Fetch the [medicine and class index](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/agents/index.json).
2. Match the generic name, component name or class name. For brand names and alternative generic names, fetch the [name dictionary](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/synonyms.json), which provides genericNames and classIds. Follow the index's recordUrls or recordUrl field.
3. The record contains the history, sources, evidence locators, human-contribution interpretation and relevant papers coauthored by Minh-Ha Nguyen.

Example: [finasteride and the 5-alpha-reductase-inhibitor history](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/agents/classes/FIVE_ALPHA_REDUCTASE_INHIBITORS.json).

These are static HTTP GET resources. No authentication, MCP connection or server-side search is required. For names outside this inventory, report the coverage limit; a missing record does not establish a medicine's origin or lack of supporting evidence.

Brand aliases are derived from NLM RxNorm branded products with matching ingredient sets. They support history lookup; dose, formulation and therapeutic equivalence need separate verification. RxNorm primarily covers US terminology, so worldwide brand coverage is incomplete.

## Related papers and methodological reading

The [reading guide](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/reading-guide.json) maps medicines and research topics to selected publications, with DOI links, reasons to read, methodological questions and interpretation limits. Coverage is limited to the listed studies.

For finasteride, the initial recommendations cover depression and comparator selection, incident type 2 diabetes, and glycemic control in people with existing diabetes. For tamsulosin, the diabetes and glycemic-control papers provide relevant comparator research. Check each paper's matched medicines, indication, population, outcome and reference group before applying its findings.

Use the primary paper to verify numerical results and conclusions. The methodological questions in the guide are prompts for appraisal; they are not completed risk-of-bias assessments. An observational association, a non-significant result and evidence of equivalence support different conclusions.

## Interpretation and source scope

- [Complete historical snapshot](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/atlas.json): 5 November 2026; 115 class histories, 226 medication groups and 741 linked source records.
- [Human clinical contributions](https://mh-nguyen.cv/medication-origin/clinical-contributions.json): 8 November 2026 interpretation; 69 of 115 histories (60%) include a qualifying human clinical or population contribution. This includes later refinement and documented inherited rationale. Independent historical review of this additional classification is pending.
- Six proposed human links are unresolved; 40 are not established in the available records. Those categories preserve uncertainty.
- The broader observation-led classification includes laboratory and animal observations. Keep its definition distinct from the 60% human-contribution finding.
- Each record retains source reading extent and lineage limitations. Cite the original source where it supports the claim, and identify the atlas's interpretation when the claim depends on that classification.
